title: India Inc not passing on gains: PM flags salary, sub-par goods
where: Front page lead, continued on page 2 (Dheeraj Mishra)
syllabus: GS4 › Ethical concerns and dilemmas in private institutions; corporate governance · GS3 › Industrial policy; effects of liberalisation; Make in India · GS2 › Consumer protection
summary: At FICCI's annual convention, the PM said industry had not passed on the corporate tax cut to workers through higher salaries or jobs, and said he was 'ashamed' of sub-par goods sold to Indian consumers.
ideas: Tax relief without sharing: corporate tax cut from 30% to 22%, yet the PM asked whether salaries or headcount had risen.
GS4 · Corporate governance / GS3 · Fiscal policy
A tax cut is a public sacrifice; corporate governance demands that its gains reach workers, not only shareholders.
Quality as an ethical duty: a captive market of 1.4 billion breeds complacency; 'our own people' are entitled to good-quality products.
GS4 · Business ethics / GS2 · Consumer protection
Selling sub-par goods because 'it will sell anyway' treats citizens as captive buyers, not stakeholders.

Self-reliance in an era of 'weaponisation of resources': India imports APIs despite being the 'Pharmacy of the World', exports iron ore but imports finished steel, has bauxite but imports aluminium alloys.
GS3 · Industrial policy / Supply chains
Raw-material exports with value-added imports show the gap between resource wealth and manufacturing depth.
Agriculture neglected by capital: India's share of global agri exports is only 2–2.5% as corporates hesitate to invest.
GS3 · Agriculture and food processing
Corporate investment in processing, procurement and export markets can turn India's farm output into an export identity.
Stakeholder nation: larger firms should lift small ones in quality and scale; a country progresses only when it respects farmers, small entrepreneurs, wealth creators and taxpayers.
GS4 · Values / GS3 · MSMEs
Growth that is shared across farmers, MSMEs and workers is both an economic and an ethical idea of progress.
keywords: Firms answer to workers, consumers and society, not only shareholders
The PM's question on salaries is a call for stakeholder capitalism over shareholder primacy.
Trust owed in return for public concessions such as tax cuts
A tax concession creates a fiduciary duty to society: the benefit is held in trust for wider welfare.
Quality slips when demand is assured
Captive-market complacency erodes quality; competitiveness abroad begins with respect for buyers at home.
Using control of inputs and supply chains as leverage
In an era of weaponisation of resources, import dependence on APIs and alloys is a strategic risk.
Moving from raw exports to finished, high-value goods
Exporting iron ore and importing steel signals the need for value-chain deepening.
data: GS3 · Fiscal policy · GS4 · Corporate governance
Despite the corporate tax cut from 30% to 22%, wage growth has lagged, the PM noted.
India's share of global agricultural exports
India's share of global agri exports is only 2–2.5%, far below its farm output.
examples: a PM asking industry to share tax gains with workers
Modi at FICCI 2026: a PM asking industry to share tax gains with workers.
strength in finished medicines, dependence in ingredients
'Pharmacy of the World' imports APIs: strength in finished medicines, dependence in ingredients.
Iron ore out, steel in: resource wealth without manufacturing depth.
consumer dignity as a business value
GS4 · Business ethics · GS2 · Consumer protection
PM 'ashamed' of sub-par goods: consumer dignity as a business value.
pyqs: Moral integrity and professional efficiency in corporate governance.
Is CSR efficient and sufficient for the corporate sector's social role?
CSR makes companies more profitable and sustainable.
Case: food company sells rejected export products in the domestic market.
Satyam scandal and changes in corporate governance.
Companies Act 2013, CSR and inclusive growth.
Corporate lobbies, pluralism and the convergence of wealth and power.

trend.t: Corporate ethics questions began with law and compliance (Companies Act CSR 2013, Satyam 2015), moved to whether CSR pays or suffices (2017, 2022), and then to the character of business itself: moral integrity in corporate governance (2023) and corporate wealth's hold on democracy (GS2, 2026). Case studies (2016, 2018, 2020, 2021, 2024) repeatedly test profit against people: workers, consumers, environment.
trend.watch: CSR and corporate governance recur almost every alternate year in GS4, and 2021's case on selling export rejects at home is the same quality-for-own-citizens issue the PM raised.
focus: Stakeholder vs shareholder model of corporate governance
Fair wages and sharing of gains with workers
Consumer rights and quality as business ethics
Limits of mandated CSR vs voluntary corporate conscience

potential: "Corporate governance is not only about compliance with law but about the moral obligation to share gains with stakeholders." Discuss with reference to recent concerns over wages and product quality. (10 marks)
What ethical issues arise when businesses sell lower-quality products in a captive domestic market? Suggest measures to build a culture of quality. (10 marks)
Examine the ethical responsibilities of industry when it receives public concessions such as tax cuts. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Corporate governance is not only about compliance with law but about the moral obligation to share gains with stakeholders." Discuss with reference to recent concerns over wages and product quality.
parts: Why gains are not shared: challenges

answer.t: Addressing FICCI in November 2026, the PM said industry had not passed on the corporate tax cut (30% to 22%) to workers and was selling sub-par goods at home.

pts.t: A firm draws on workers, consumers and public resources, so it owes them a fair share, not only its shareholders.
pts.ex: PM: 'Have you increased the salaries of your employees?'

pts.t: Tax relief is a sacrifice by the public exchequer; using it only for profit breaks an implicit social contract.
pts.ex: Corporate tax cut to 22% without matching wage gains.

pts.t: Quality is respect for the buyer; a captive market is not a licence for poor goods.
pts.ex: PM: 'Are our own people not entitled to good-quality products?'

pts.k: Integrity over the letter of law
pts.t: Legal minimums such as mandated CSR can coexist with unfair wages; conscience must go further.
pts.ex: Satyam (2009): compliant on paper, fraudulent in substance.

pts.t: Large firms can mentor MSMEs on quality and scale.
pts.ex: PM asks big companies to help smaller ones develop quality.

answer.h: Why gains are not shared: challenges

pts.t: Quarterly profit pressure favours buybacks and dividends over wages.
pts.ex: Tax savings retained as profit, not shared as pay.

pts.t: Abundant labour keeps bargaining power and wages low.
pts.ex: Informal and contract work in manufacturing.

pts.t: Patchy standards and testing let poor goods pass.
pts.ex: GS4-2021 case: export rejects sold domestically.

pts.t: Tie concessions to jobs, wages and quality benchmarks, as in output-linked schemes.
Mandatory standards, consumer redress and 'zero defect' as a value.
pts.ex: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and BIS standards.

pts.t: Boards that measure fair wages and customer trust, not only profit.
pts.ex: Gandhi's idea of trusteeship, recalled by the PM.

answer.t: Good corporate governance is measured by who shares in the gains; profit with fair wages and fair goods is the ethic India's growth needs.

title: With decline in poverty, shift focus — from free food to nutritional security
where: Ideas page, page 9 (Ashok Gulati, Ritika Juneja and Sulakshana Rao, ICRIER)
syllabus: GS3 › Food security; public distribution system; buffer stocks · GS3 › Agriculture: soil health, biofortification · GS2 › Issues relating to poverty and hunger; malnutrition
summary: Using the World Bank brief, the authors argue that with extreme poverty at 2.6%, free grain to 81 crore people under PM-GKY should be rationalised and reoriented to nutrition: food coupons, biofortified staples and healthier soils.
ideas: Poverty fell faster after 2004: growth up, population growth down.
GS3 · Growth and poverty
Fewer mouths share each rupee of growth.
Farm growth cuts poverty 2.5x more (World Development Report 2008).
GS3 · Agriculture
Invest in farms to cut poverty.
Free grain to ~81 crore needs rationalising at 2.6% extreme poverty.
GS3 · Food subsidies
Target the poorest, price the rest.
From calories to nutrition: coupons, biofortified staples, healthier soils.
GS3 · Nutrition security
Nutrition starts in the soil.
keywords: Access to a diet with adequate nutrients, not just calories
India has achieved food security; nutrition security is the next goal.
Carbon in soil that sustains fertility and nutrient uptake
India's SOC of about 0.3% against a desirable 1.5–2% explains nutrient-poor grain.
Breeding crops richer in micronutrients like iron and zinc
Biofortified wheat and rice can fight hidden hunger through the PDS.
Free wheat and rice fill stomachs but not the gap of hidden hunger.
data: India's soil organic carbon against the desirable level
World Food Laureate Rattan Lal (cited by the authors)
India's soil organic carbon is around 0.3%, against a desirable 1.5–2%, says Rattan Lal.
How much more potent agricultural growth is in reducing poverty than other growth
The WDR 2008 found farm growth at least 2.5 times more effective at cutting poverty.
examples: iron and zinc through the PDS
Biofortified wheat and rice: iron and zinc through the PDS.
'Teach to fish': empower, don't create dependence.
pyqs: Malnutrition as challenge of social equity, human development, welfare governance.
Breaking the vicious cycle of poverty and malnutrition for human capital.
Millets for health and nutritional security.

trend.t: Food questions moved from distribution (PDS reforms, 2019 and 2022; NFSA, 2021) to nutrition (millets, 2024; poverty–malnutrition cycle, 2024) and in 2026 malnutrition as a challenge of equity and welfare governance.
trend.watch: Malnutrition was asked in 2024 and 2026, and PDS in 2019 and 2022, so the shift 'from food security to nutrition security' is a must-study theme.
focus: Nutrition: millets, pulses, milk and eggs

potential: "India has moved from food scarcity to food security; it must now move to nutrition security." Discuss. (15 marks)
Examine the case for rationalising free food grain under PM-GKY. (10 marks)

practice.q: "India has moved from food scarcity to food security; it must now move to nutrition security." Discuss.

answer.t: The World Bank's October 2026 brief shows India's extreme poverty fell to 2.6% in 2023, yet child malnutrition remains high, so the challenge has moved from calories to nutrients.

pts.t: The National Food Security Act, 2013 made food a right.
Free grain to about 81 crore people.
pts.ex: PM-GKY extended for five years from 2024.

pts.t: Allocations were enhanced to 10 kg per person per month during Covid.
Transfers contributed to falling poverty.
PDS gives wheat and rice, not diverse diets.
pts.ex: Millets, pulses, milk and eggs largely outside PDS.

pts.t: Wheat and rice are deficient in iron and zinc.
Low soil organic carbon reduces nutrient content.
Under-five malnutrition remains very high.
Free grain for over half the population costs heavily.
Flat real farm wages limit diet diversity.
pts.ex: World Bank brief on real earnings.

pts.t: Free for the poorest, part-price for others.
Let families buy healthier foods from designated stores.
Iron- and zinc-rich wheat and rice in the PDS.
Raise soil organic carbon through organic matter and crop diversity.
Shift incentives from rice and wheat to pulses and millets.
Link PDS with Poshan, ICDS and school meals.

answer.t: Viksit Bharat cannot be built on full stomachs and empty plates of nutrients; nutrition security must start in the soil and end on the child's plate.

title: In fertiliser sales dip, a lesson for policymakers
syllabus: GS3 › Agriculture: inputs, subsidies, food security; Inflation; Effects of climate change · GS1 › Monsoon and El Niño
summary: Fertiliser sales fell in April–September as a 'super strong' El Niño weakened the monsoon; the editorial warns of rabi losses and food inflation and asks policymakers to treat climate and geopolitical shocks as the new normal.
ideas: Falling fertiliser sales signal farm distress: sales of all fertilisers, including cheap urea, fell despite higher production and imports, because weak rains gave farmers little reason to apply them.
GS3 · Agriculture inputs
Falling fertiliser offtake despite ample supply is an early indicator of farm distress and lower yields.
El Niño hits both seasons: a deficient monsoon hurt kharif; a dry October and an El Niño expected to persist till early 2027 mean less soil moisture and a warmer winter for rabi.
GS1 · El Niño and monsoon / GS3 · Agriculture
A strong El Niño can hurt both kharif and rabi through deficient rain, low soil moisture and warmer winters.
Climate shocks become food inflation: food inflation has risen sharply this year, and the 2023–24 food-inflation episode was also driven by a long El Niño.
GS3 · Inflation
Food inflation in India is often a weather-driven supply shock that monetary policy alone cannot fix.

Short term, use trade tools: duty-free imports of pulses, raw sugar and cotton till March 31, scrapping customs duty on crude palm and soyabean oil, and a longer window so importers can contract large volumes.
GS3 · Food security / Trade policy
Timely, predictable import windows can cushion domestic shortages and keep food prices stable.

Long term, a 'default reality' mindset: treat climate change and geopolitical tension as baseline conditions; invest in climate-smart breeding, efficient use of water, fertiliser and energy, and reorder an inefficient subsidy regime, which is a political more than an economic challenge.
GS3 · Climate-smart agriculture / Subsidy reform
Treating climate shocks as the default, not the exception, demands climate-smart farming and courageous subsidy reform.
keywords: Unusually intense Pacific warming that weakens India's monsoon
A super-strong El Niño threatens two crop seasons, not one.
Actual use of fertiliser by farmers
Low nutrient offtake today signals lower yields tomorrow.
Prices rising because of output shortfalls, not demand
El Niño-driven food inflation is supply-side, so it needs supply-side answers.
Farming that adapts to and withstands climate stress
Climate-smart breeding and efficient input use make farms resilient to El Niño years.
Planning for shocks as the normal condition
Policy must treat climate and geopolitical shocks as default realities, not rare risks.
More crop per drop, per kg of fertiliser, per unit of energy
Raising input-use efficiency is cheaper and greener than raising input subsidies.
examples: Weak monsoon, falling fertiliser sales, risk to rabi, rising food inflation
GS1 · El Niño and monsoon · GS3 · Climate change and food security, inflation · Essay
The 2026 El Niño shows how one ocean-atmosphere event travels from the Pacific to farmers' fields and household food bills.
A long El Niño also drove India's last major food-inflation episode
GS3 · Inflation and limits of monetary policy · GS3 · Disaster preparedness
Back-to-back El Niño inflation episodes show climate shocks recur, so preparedness must be permanent.
Duty-free windows for pulses, sugar and edible oils to make up shortfalls
GS1 · Globalisation · GS3 · Food security, trade policy
Calibrated imports show how global markets can buffer domestic climate shocks: a positive face of globalisation.
pyqs: Persistent food inflation and the limits of RBI policy.
Climate change and food security in tropical countries.
Farm subsidies and the WTO Agreement on Agriculture.
Subsidies, cropping pattern and small farmers.

trend.t: Food inflation came first through farm markets (APMCs, 2014) and returned in 2024 as persistent food inflation and the limits of RBI policy. Climate and food security moved from impacts on tropical countries (2023) to climate-smart agriculture (2026). Farm subsidies recur in 2013, 2015, 2017, 2023 and 2026, increasingly with a WTO angle.
trend.watch: Farm subsidies are near-annual, and food inflation and climate-smart agriculture are recent. Prepare one integrated answer: climate shock, then food inflation, then subsidy and trade response.
focus: Supply-side food inflation and limits of monetary policy
Fertiliser subsidy reform and input efficiency

potential: "Food inflation in India is increasingly a climate problem, not a monetary one." Discuss. (15 marks)
How does El Niño affect Indian agriculture across the kharif and rabi seasons? Suggest adaptation measures. (10 marks)
Examine the case for reforming India's fertiliser subsidy regime in the context of climate change. (10 marks)

practice.q: How does El Niño affect Indian agriculture across the kharif and rabi seasons? Suggest adaptation measures.

answer.t: A 'super strong' El Niño this year has weakened the monsoon, and fertiliser sales fell in April–September even as supply rose.

pts.t: Weak rains cut kharif sowing and yields in rainfed regions.
Farmers apply less fertiliser, lowering productivity.
A dry post-monsoon hurts rabi sowing.
Heat at grain-filling reduces wheat yields.
Shortfalls push up prices of pulses, oils and vegetables.
Lower incomes reduce rural demand.
Drought- and heat-tolerant varieties.
Micro-irrigation and soil-health-based fertiliser use.
Timely, predictable duty-free import windows.
Weather-based advisories and crop insurance.
Shift support from inputs to resilience.

answer.t: With El Niño now a recurring visitor, India must plan for climate shocks as the default and build farms that can withstand them.
